'''''Lythrum salicaria''''' or '''purple-loosestrife'''<ref name="BSBI">{{cite web | title=Purple-loosestrife ''Lythrum salicaria'' L. | website=PlantAtlas | url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.vmn | access-date=2025-07-11}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | title=''Lythrum salicaria'' L. Common name: Purple-loosestrife | website=Plants of the World Online | url=https://powo.science.kew.org/results?q=Lythrum%20salicaria | access-date=2025-07-11}}</ref><ref name=fnwe>Flora of NW Europe: [http://ip30.eti.uva.nl/BIS/flora.php?selected=beschrijving&menuentry=soorten&id=3030 ''Lythrum salicaria''] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080219215020/http://ip30.eti.uva.nl/BIS/flora.php?selected=beschrijving&menuentry=soorten&id=3030 |date=2008-02-19 }}</ref> is a [[flowering plant]] belonging to the family [[Lythraceae]]. It should not be confused with other plants sharing the name loosestrife that are members of the genus ''[[Lysimachia]]'' in the family [[Primulaceae]]. This [[herbaceous]] [[perennial plant]] is native to temperate regions of Europe, Asia, northern Africa, and eastern Australia.<ref name="POWO"/>

==Etymology and other names==
The generic name ''Lythrum'' is derived from the Greek 'lythron', meaning blood, in reference to the flower colour in some species.<ref name= "Gledhill">Gledhill D. 1985. ''The Names of Plants''. Cambridge University Press {{ISBN|978-0-5213-6675-5}}</ref> The [[specific epithet]] ''salicaria'' probably derives from the similarity of the leaves to those of willows or ''[[Salix]]'' species,<ref>{{cite book | last=Chauvet | first=Michel | title=Etymologia botanica | publisher=Éditions Biotope | publication-place=Mèze | date=2024-07-31 | isbn=978-2-36662-319-2 | language=fr | page=}}</ref> though Linnaeus did not specify this in his choice of the name.

The English [[calque]] 'loosestrife' first appeared in written form in the 16th century. It was coined by English naturalist [[William Turner (naturalist)|William Turner]] in his 1548 work ''A New Herball'', in which he states: "''Lycimachia purpurea'', … may in englishe be called red loosstryfe or purple losestryfe".{{efn|Turner treated this species and [[yellow loosestrife]] (now ''Lysimachia vulgaris'') in the same genus ''Lycimachia'' [sic]}}<ref>''Oxford English Dictionary'' L: 438.</ref>

Purple-loosestrife was referred to several times as 'long purples' by [[John Clare]], such as in his 1821 poem ''The Wildflower Nosegay'':<ref>Grigson G. 1974. ''A Dictionary of English Plant Names.'' Allen Lane. {{isbn|978-0713904420}}.</ref>

{{Blockquote|"Where on the water op'd the lily buds

And fine long purples shadow'd in the lake..."

|Volume II of ''The Village Minstrel and Other Poems'', John Clare, pg. 133}}

==Description==
''Lythrum salicaria'' can grow {{cvt|1-2|m|ftin|abbr=on}} tall, forming extensive [[clonal colony|clonal colonies]], with numerous erect stems growing from a single woody root mass. The stems are reddish-purple and square in cross-section. The leaves are [[lanceolate]], {{convert|3–10|cm|in|frac=2}} long and {{convert|5–15|mm|in|frac=16}} broad, downy and [[Sessility (botany)|sessile]], and arranged opposite or in whorls of three.

[[File:Блатия 2.jpg|thumb|right|''L. salicaria'' flowers]]
The flowers are reddish purple, {{convert|10–20|mm|in|frac=4}} in diameter, with six petals (occasionally five) and 12 stamens, and are clustered tightly in [[verticillaster]]s in the [[axil]]s of [[bract]]s or leaves. There are [[Heterostyly|three different flower types]], with the stamens and style of different lengths, short, medium or long; each flower type can only be pollinated by one of the other types, not the same type, thus ensuring cross-pollination between different plants.<ref name=fnwe/><ref name=foc>{{cite web |website=Flora of China vol. 13 |page=282 |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200014658 |title=''Lythrum salicaria''|year=2007|access-date=27 October 2022}}</ref><ref name=blamey>Blamey, M. & Grey-Wilson, C. (1989). ''The Illustrated Flora of Britain and Northern Europe''. Hodder & Stoughton.  {{ISBN|0-340-40170-2}}.</ref> For instance, if the [[pistil]] is medium length, then the [[stamens]] will be long and short, but not medium.<ref>{{cite book | last= Meeuse Ph.D.| first=B.J.D. | date= 1961| title= The Story of Pollination | location= New York | publisher= Ronald Press Co. | page= 174- 175 with illust.}}</ref> The flowers are visited by many types of insects, and can be characterised by a generalised [[pollination syndrome]].<ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1111/plb.12328| pmid = 25754608| title = Competition for pollinators and intra-communal spectral dissimilarity of flowers| journal = Plant Biology| volume = 18| issue = 1| pages = 56–62| year = 2015| last1 = Van Der Kooi | first1 = C. J.| last2 = Pen | first2 = I.| last3 = Staal | first3 = M.| last4 = Stavenga | first4 = D. G.| last5 = Elzenga | first5 = J. T. M.| url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/273158762| hdl = 11370/caee8d0d-9724-4056-9d45-93162a5a7afc| hdl-access = free}}</ref>

The fruit is a small {{convert|3–4|mm|in|frac=64}} [[capsule (fruit)|capsule]]<ref>Clapham, A.R., Tutin, T.G. and Warburg, R.F. 1968. ''Excursion Flora of the British Isles''. Cambridge University Press. {{ISBN|0 521 04656 4}}</ref> containing numerous minute [[seed]]s. Flowering lasts throughout the summer. When the seeds are mature, the leaves often turn bright red through dehydration in early autumn; the red autumn colour may last for almost two weeks. The dead stalks from previous growing seasons are brown.<ref name=fnwe/><ref name=foc/><ref name=blamey/>

[[File:Блатия 4.jpg|thumb|right|''L. salicaria'' leaves]]
''L. salicaria'' is very variable in leaf shape and degree of hairiness, and a number of subspecies and varieties have been described, but it is now generally regarded as monotypic with none of these variants being considered of botanical significance.<ref name="POWO"/> The species ''[[Lythrum intermedium]]'' <small>Ledeb. ex Colla</small> has often been considered [[synonym (taxonomy)|synonymous]] in the past,<ref name=fnwe/><ref name=blamey/><ref name=fe>{{cite web |website=Flora Europaea |title=''Lithium salicaria'' |url=https://websites.rbge.org.uk/cgi-bin/nph-readbtree.pl/feout?FAMILY_XREF=&GENUS_XREF=Lythrum&SPECIES_XREF=salicaria&TAXON_NAME_XREF=&RANK= |access-date=27 October 2022|publisher=Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh}}</ref> but is now treated as a separate species, from Central Asia, by the ''[[Plants of the World Online]]'' database.<ref name="POWO2">{{cite POWO |title=''Lythrum intermedium'' Fisch. ex Colla |id= 553739-1 |access-date=2025-07-11}}</ref>

==Distribution==
''Lythrum salicaria'' is native to Europe, temperate Asia, northern Africa, and Australia.<ref name="POWO"/><ref name=foc/><ref name=fe/><ref name=mc>Med-Checklist: [ ''Lythrum salicaria'']</ref><ref name="APNI">{{cite web |url=https://id.biodiversity.org.au/name/apni/82727 |title=''Lythrum salicaria'' |website=[[Australian Plant Name Index]] (APNI) |publisher=Centre for Plant Biodiversity Research, [[Australian Government]] |access-date=15 March 2023}}</ref> It is also naturalised in many temperate parts of the world, including parts of southern Africa, North America, and South America.<ref name="POWO"/><ref name = GRIN>{{GRIN}}</ref> The species was thought to be a recent introduction to Australia, but pre-colonial pollen samples have been found in New South Wales, indicating natural colonisation before modern human plant introductions;<ref>{{cite book|title=Wetland Weeds: Causes, Cures and Compromises|last=Romanowski|first=Nick|page=34|isbn=978-0-643-10395-5|year=2011|publisher=CSIRO Publishing|location=Collingwood, Victoria}}</ref> the question is considered unresolved by Australian authorities.<ref name="Vicflora" >{{Cite web|url=https://vicflora.rbg.vic.gov.au/flora/taxon/3735e1b9-28f1-446b-8265-5edb6c021bef|title=''Lythrum salicaria'' L. Purple Loosestrife|website=VicFlora|publisher=[[Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria]]|last=Stajsic|first=Val|date=27 March 2018|access-date=27 October 2022}}</ref>

==Ecology==
Found in ditches, [[wet meadow]]s and marshes and along sides of lakes.<ref>Webb, D.A., Parnell, J. and Doogue, D. 1996. ''An Irish Flora''. Dundalk, Ireland: Dundalgan Press (W.Tempest) Ltd.  {{ISBN|0-85221-131-7}}.</ref> In North America, purple-loosestrife can invade [[sedge meadows]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://ecology.fnal.gov/sedge-meadow/|website=Fermilab|publisher=Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory|title=Sedge Meadow|access-date=29 October 2022}}</ref>

==Associated insects==
The flowers are pollinated by long-tongued insects, including [[bee]]s and [[butterfly|butterflies]].<ref name=blamey/>

A number of [[insect]]s use ''Lythrum salicaria'' as a food resource.

The black-margined loosestrife beetle ''[[Galerucella calmariensis]]'' is a brown beetle with a black line on its thorax. The adult feeds on the leaves of the plant, producing characteristic round holes. Its larvae destroy tender leaf buds and strip the tissue from the leaves. The golden loosestrife beetle ''[[Galerucella pusilla]]'' is nearly identical to ''G. calmariensis'', but usually lacks the black thoracic line. Its feeding habits are also quite similar to the other leaf beetle.

The loosestrife root weevil ''[[Hylobius transversovittatus]]'' is a large red nocturnal weevil, which spends its nights feeding on leaves and leaf buds. The larvae emerge from their eggs and immediately burrow into the root of the plant, which they feed on continuously for over a year. This root damage stunts the plant's growth and ability to create seeds. If several larvae inhabit the same root, the plant can be killed.

The loosestrife flower weevil ''[[Nanophyes marmoratus]]'' is a tiny weevil which lays a single egg in each flower. When the larvae emerge they eat the flowers' ovaries, and the plant is unable to create seeds. The larvae usually proceed to hollow out the flower buds and use them as safe places to pupate.

[[Caterpillar]]s of the engrailed moth (''[[Ectropis crepuscularia]]''), a polyphagous [[Geometridae|geometer moth]], also feed on purple-loosestrife.

==Cultivation, uses and impact==
It has been used as an [[astringent]] [[herbal medicine|medicinal herb]] to treat [[diarrhea]] and [[dysentery]]; it is considered safe to use for all ages, including babies.<ref name=pfaf>Plants for a Future: [http://www.pfaf.org/database/plants.php?Lythrum+salicaria ''Lythrum salicaria'']</ref> It is also cultivated as an [[ornamental plant]] in gardens, and is particularly associated with damp, poorly drained locations such as marshes, bogs and watersides. However, it will tolerate drier conditions. The flowers are showy and bright, and a number of [[cultivar]]s have been selected for variation in flower colour, including:
* 'Atropurpureum' with dark purple flowers
* 'Brightness' with deep pink flowers
* 'Happy' with red flowers on a short ({{convert|60|cm|in|0|abbr=on|disp=or}}) stem
* 'Purple Spires' with purple flowers on a tall stem
* 'Roseum Superbum' with large pink flowers.<ref name=rhs>Huxley, A., ed. (1992). ''New RHS Dictionary of Gardening''. Macmillan {{ISBN|0-333-47494-5}}.</ref>

The cultivars 'Blush'<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/102703/i-Lythrum-salicaria-i-Blush/Details
| title = RHS Plantfinder - ''Lythrum salicaria'' 'Blush' | access-date = 25 March 2018}}</ref> with blush-pink flowers, and 'Feuerkerze'<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Lythrum salicaria'' 'Feuerkerze'|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/116301/lythrum-salicaria-feuerkerze-/details-beta|access-date=27 December 2020|archive-date=8 September 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230908040352/https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/116301/lythrum-salicaria-feuerkerze-/details-beta}}</ref> with rose-red flowers have gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web  | url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 62 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 25 March 2018}}</ref>

It has also been introduced in many areas of North America by [[bee keeper]]s,{{citation needed|date=December 2020}} due to its abundance of flowers which provide an important source of [[nectar]].<ref name="regulation">

===As an invasive species===

Purple-loosestrife has been introduced into temperate [[New Zealand]] and [[North America]] where it is now widely [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]] (spreading on its own) and officially listed in some controlling agents. Infestations may rarely result in dramatic disruption in water flow in rivers and canals, and the life cycles of organisms from waterfowl to amphibians to algae being affected.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Anderson |first=Mark G. |date=1995-03-01 |title=Interactions betweenLythrum salicaria and native organisms: A critical review |journal=Environmental Management |language=en |volume=19 |issue=2 |pages=225–231 |doi=10.1007/BF02471992 |issn=1432-1009}}</ref>

A single plant may produce up to 2.7 million tiny seeds annually.<ref>{{cite web|title=Non-native Invasive Freshwater Plants - Purple Loosestrife (''Lythrum salicaria'')|url=http://www.ecy.wa.gov/programs/wq/plants/weeds/aqua009.html|access-date=6 June 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160707014743/http://www.ecy.wa.gov/programs/wq/plants/weeds/aqua009.html|archive-date=7 July 2016}}</ref> Easily carried by wind and water, the seeds germinate in moist soils after overwintering. The plant can also sprout anew from pieces of root left in the soil or water. Once established, loosestrife stands are difficult and costly to remove by mechanical and chemical means.

However, research about how invasive plants are portrayed in media indicate that the threat from loosestrife and other infamous invasive plants is driven more by media attention than science.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Woodworth |first1=Elena |last2=Tian |first2=Amy |last3=Blair |first3=Kaleigh |last4=Pullen |first4=Jamie |last5=Lefcheck |first5=Jonathan S. |last6=Parker |first6=John D. |title=Media myopia distorts public interest in US invasive plants |journal=Biological Invasions |date=October 2023 |volume=25 |issue=10 |pages=3193–3205 |doi=10.1007/s10530-023-03101-8 |doi-access=free}}</ref> While the species does have negative impacts on the natural environment the scientific literature supports a much more modest assessment of how bad it is outside its native range and that resources would be better spent on preventing disturbance of wetlands than on the removal of purple-loosestrife.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lavoie |first1=Claude |title=Should we care about purple loosestrife? The history of an invasive plant in North America |journal=Biological Invasions |date=July 2010 |volume=12 |issue=7 |pages=1967–1999 |doi=10.1007/s10530-009-9600-7}}</ref>

Plants marketed under the name "European wand loosestrife" (''L. virgatum'') are the same species despite the different name. In some cases the plants sold are sterile.{{cn|date=July 2025}}

In North America, purple-loosestrife may be distinguished from similar native plants (e.g., [[fireweed]] ''Chamerion angustifolium'', [[Vervain|blue vervain]] ''Verbena hastata'', [[Liatris]] ''Liatris'' spp., and [[spiraea]] (''[[Spiraea douglasii]]'') by its angular stalks which are square in outline, as well as by its leaves, which are in pairs that alternate at right angle and are not serrated.

====Biological control====
Purple-loosestrife provides a model of successful [[biological pest control]]. Research began in 1985 and today the plant is managed well with a number of insects that feed on it. Five species of [[beetle]] use purple-loosestrife as their natural food source, and they can do significant damage to the plant. The beetles used as biological control agents include two species of [[leaf beetle]]: ''[[Galerucella calmariensis]]'' and ''[[Galerucella pusilla]]''; and three species of [[weevil]]: ''[[Hylobius transversovittatus]]'', ''[[Nanophyes breves]]'', and ''[[Nanophyes marmoratus]]''. Infestations of either of the ''[[Galerucella]]'' species is extremely effective in wiping out a stand of purple-loosestrife, defoliating up to 100% of the plants in an area. The moth ''[[Ectropis crepuscularia]]'' is [[polyphagous]] and a [[pest (organism)|pest]] species itself, and unsuitable for biological control.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Wilson|first1=Linda M.|last2=Schwarzlaender|first2=Mark|last3=Blossey|first3=Bernd|last4=Randall|first4=Carol Bell |year=2004 |title=Biology and Biological Control of Purple Loosestrife|location=Morgantown, WV|publisher=USDA Forest Health Technology Enterprise Team|url=https://bugwoodcloud.org/resource/files/6225.pdf|access-date=27 October 2022}}</ref>
